title: Approached me to let them use my phone on a lonely road (asked me to dial the number if I cannot trust him or give him my charger)
body_text: I am a girl and was with my guy friend who is pretty well built and we were just about to sit in my car parked in a pretty secluded lane in a very posh neighbourhood known for having lots of cafes and eateries in Pune. This random guy who was very well dressed and had fluent English with a slight accent as well (I don’t know his name but he was about 5’10, medium built, fair skinned with brownish gel wax styled hair and wore a chain that atleast looked like a gold chain and one ring that looked like a gold ring too. He was dressed in linen pants and a pink t shirt) came to us with a very old iPhone maybe an iPhone 6 or something in his hand saying his battery was over and he wanted to make a call. We said he can go to any cafe around and ask for a charging and they’ll let him charge as they always have various chargers there. He kept insisting that his friend was on his way to this neighbourhood but now that his battery is over he doesn’t know how to communicate with this friend. While he was talking we sat in the car. Then he said can you let me charge my phone in your car and can you yourself dial my friends number on your phone and give me the phone if you think I will run away with your phone I’ll sit in your car and you can lock the car while I speak. I said I’m sorry I’m not comfortable with you sitting in my car and asked him to move as he was blocking my way and I couldn’t take out my car. He then randomly showed me his wallet saying “look I have so many cards (he had 2-3 bank cards in his wallet) and I’m not a scammer please help me I actually have an iPhone too the same as you”. My iPhone is one of the newer ones with a c type charger but I did have an old cord compatible with older iPhones which I use to charge my AirPods. We were basically not feeling like doing any of this because why take a risk so we just said sorry and asked him to go to the nearest police station which was 500 metres away and they will help him make a call. He then said “I don’t have battery in my phone to book a cab or pay by UPI and can you atleast help me with some money.” I said I’m not carrying cash but I can call the cops to take him to the station from here to help him. He said let me see I will figure out and he got out of my way. I just quickly turned on the car and left for home. I would’ve probably thought of helping if it was not a secluded road so I don’t know but is this some known kind of scam? Did I avoid a scam? Or did I actually not help a genuine person? If he was a scammer he was obviously not someone who was interested in 100-200 bucks so why was he asking for some money to help with rickshaw/cab? Has anybody else experienced this?/knows about this?

Origins Network / LGNS Warning Report

**High-risk / extreme caution**

This page is a plain-English warning summary about public red flags connected to Origins Network / LGNS. It is not a court finding. It is a due-diligence summary meant to help people slow down, verify, and avoid possible fraud.

# Scam scorecard

# Red flags

* **Contract-risk warning from CoinGecko / GoPlus:** public page says the contract is unverified and warns the owner can potentially change behavior including disabling sells, changing fees, minting, and transferring tokens.
* **Admin control in verified Polygon contract:** code includes `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`, an admin-only `setRatio(...)` function for fees, and a vault-only `mint(...)` function.
* **Supply inconsistency:** CoinGecko shows total supply of 150,375 and max supply infinity, while GeckoTerminal says the largest holder owns 1.3B LGNS.
* **Large reported volume with unclear economics:** GeckoTerminal reports roughly $60.88M 24h volume and 963.26K 24h transactions.
* **Severe historical drawdown:** CoinGecko shows a current price around $6.13 versus an all-time high of $84.63.

# Yellow flags

* The project presents a broad system story around a “decentralized financial operating system,” which can make it harder for regular buyers to verify the actual value engine.
* Public tracker data do not line up cleanly across sites, making fair valuation harder.
* Very high trading activity deserves extra scrutiny when supply and holder data are hard to reconcile.

# What does not prove fraud by itself

* GeckoTerminal says the pool contract is verified and shows no indication of a honeypot.
* A pool existing for years and still trading does not automatically make a project safe, but it does mean the warning should be framed carefully and honestly.

# Practical takeaway

If a project has admin-controlled fees, mint permissions, contradictory supply data, and a giant drawdown, that is enough reason for most people to step back and avoid committing money until the team can reconcile the facts in a clear, independently verifiable way.

# Sources used in the warning

* CoinGecko LGNS page
* PolygonScan verified contract page for `0xeB51D9A39AD5EEF215dC0Bf39a8821ff804A0F01`
* GeckoTerminal LGNS/DAI pool page for `0x882df4b0fb50a229c3b4124eb18c759911485bfb`
